subject: 재산권과 공유지의 문제
title: Ownership and the commons
content: A resource that everyone may use and nobody owns will often be depleted, since each user gains the whole of what she takes while bearing only a fraction of the cost. This argument is widely cited to justify private ownership, and it has the form of a proof rather than an observation. Political philosophy has nevertheless questioned whether it establishes what its users suppose. The argument assumes that users cannot communicate or bind one another, and where that assumption fails the conclusion does not follow. Extensive fieldwork has documented commons managed successfully for centuries, with rules about who may take, how much, and when, enforced by the users themselves rather than by an owner or a state. Such arrangements share features that can be listed, among them clear boundaries, graduated sanctions, and forums for resolving disputes. What follows is not that private ownership is unjustified but that the choice is wider than two options. A resource may be held privately, held by a state, or governed by its users under rules they made, and each arrangement performs well under some conditions and badly under others. Treating the commons as inevitably tragic therefore forecloses an alternative that the evidence shows to work, and the moral question of who should decide remains open in every case.

subject: 고대의 도량형과 표준의 성립
title: How ancient measures became standard
content: Ancient weights recovered from dug settlements are often consistent within a small fraction, and yet the sets from neighbouring regions rarely agree with one another. This pattern tells us that standard measures arose locally and repeatedly rather than spreading from any single source. A community that traded within itself needed one standard, and it had no reason to take up anyone else's. Where a larger power emerged, the picture changes. Ancient rulers who collected in kind needed to know what a measure of grain came to, so quarrels about quantity became quarrels about what was owed, and the law codes of the period treat false weights with penalties that are notably harsh. Standard measures were at times kept in temples, where their care carried religious force beside legal force, and copies checked against them went out to the markets. What the dug sequence shows is that unification followed political reach rather than trading ease. Districts drawn into a larger ancient state take up its weights within a generation, whereas districts that stayed outside keep their own for centuries. Historians therefore use the spread of weight standards as a separate map of how far an ancient power truly reached, since it records practice rather than the claims made in inscriptions.

subject: 법과 도덕의 분리 가능성
title: Whether law and morality come apart
content: A law may be valid and yet unjust, and whether this is possible has divided legal philosophy for a long time. One tradition holds that the existence of a law is one question and its merit another, so an evil statute properly enacted remains law while deserving condemnation. The separation preserves clear thinking, since it lets us say that a rule binds legally while denying that it binds morally. A rival tradition holds that law is inherently a moral enterprise, so a sufficiently unjust rule fails to be law at all rather than being bad law. Its defenders point out that legal reasoning is saturated with moral concepts, and that judges deciding hard cases appeal to justice rather than merely reporting what was enacted. On this view the separation misdescribes what courts actually do. Much of the disagreement concerns what turns on the answer. Separationists argue that their view makes criticism easier, because a citizen who recognizes a rule as valid law can still refuse it on moral grounds, whereas defining injustice out of law leaves no vocabulary for the case. Their opponents reply that the separation encourages officials to treat validity as settling the matter. Both sides therefore claim the practical high ground, which suggests the dispute is partly about what a theory of law is for.

subject: 중세 유럽의 성채와 정주 형태
title: Castles and where medieval people settled
content: A medieval castle is usually described as a military structure, and excavation of the settlements around such sites shows that it was also a magnet. Villages cluster beneath the walls, roads bend toward the gate, and the fields laid out nearby follow a plan that assumes the castle was already there. The archaeological sequence therefore records the fortification arriving first and the settlement forming around it. What drew people was not only protection. A castle household consumed food, fuel, and craft goods continuously, so a village at its foot had a buyer that no ordinary hamlet enjoyed, and the excavated refuse from such villages shows a wider range of goods than comparable sites away from any fortification. Security and supply worked together, and neither alone explains the pattern. When a castle was abandoned, the settlement beneath it usually shrank rather than disappearing. Excavations show houses falling out of use in the quarters nearest the walls while those along the road survive, which suggests that the road had acquired a value independent of the fortification. Historians reading these sequences treat the medieval castle as a settlement event as much as a military one, and the map of surviving villages preserves the choice long after the walls came down.

subject: 거대한 수와 도덕적 직관
title: Large numbers and moral intuition
content: Our moral responses do not scale with the numbers involved, and this failure is well documented. People give as generously to save one identified child as to save thousands, and a disaster affecting a distant multitude moves us less than a single case we can picture. Moral philosophy asks whether this reveals a defect in our responses or a limit on what morality can require. One position treats the insensitivity as an error to be corrected. If each life carries equal weight, then a thousand deaths are a thousand times worse than one, and a response that fails to register the difference is simply mistaken, however natural it may be. On this view moral progress consists partly in learning to act on the arithmetic rather than on the feeling. A second position resists that conclusion. It observes that the arithmetic generates verdicts most people reject, such as the claim that a large number of minor discomforts can outweigh one person's agony, and it treats those rejections as evidence rather than as failures of nerve. Between the two lies a practical difficulty neither resolves. Institutions must make decisions at scale, and a moral psychology built for small groups gives them little guidance, so the arithmetic is used by default while remaining philosophically contested.

subject: 시장에서 거래되면 안 되는 것
title: What should not be for sale
content: Most societies place some goods outside the market, forbidding the sale of votes, of persons, and often of organs, and moral philosophy asks what principle these prohibitions share. The question is pressing because markets extend into areas they once did not reach, and each extension is defended by pointing out that both parties consent and both expect to gain. One argument against sale appeals to coercion. A person who sells a kidney because she cannot otherwise feed her children is not exercising a free choice in any meaningful sense, so the transaction ratifies a desperation that ought to be relieved instead. Critics answer that forbidding the sale leaves her worse off, since it removes an option without addressing the desperation, and that the objection is really to poverty rather than to markets. A second argument appeals to corruption rather than to consent. Some goods are altered by being priced, so that a friendship bought is not a friendship and an honour purchased is not an honour, and putting such things on sale degrades what they are. This objection survives the reply about consent, since it does not depend on anyone being pressured. Its difficulty is saying which goods have this character, and moral philosophy has produced no criterion that settles the contested cases.

subject: 문자 기록 이전의 인구 추정법
title: Estimating ancient populations without records
content: No census survives for most of human history, and yet historians of ancient and prehistoric periods routinely state population figures. Those figures come from proxies, and understanding the proxies matters more than memorizing the numbers, because each one carries assumptions that can fail. The commonest method counts dwellings at an excavated settlement and multiplies by an assumed household size. That assumption is doing enormous work. Household size varies with inheritance customs, with mortality, and with whether unmarried adults live separately, so a factor drawn from one society and applied to another can be wrong by half. Archaeologists therefore prefer sites where the excavation is extensive enough to show how many buildings were occupied simultaneously, since a settlement rebuilt over centuries contains far more houses than it ever held families. Other proxies avoid dwellings entirely. Cemeteries yield estimates from the number of burials and the period they span, and the area under cultivation yields a ceiling from what the land could feed. Each proxy has its own bias, and the practice now is to compare several rather than to trust one. Where they converge the estimate is reported with some confidence, and where they diverge the divergence itself becomes the finding that historians report.

subject: 개연성과 합리적 믿음
title: Probability and what it is rational to believe
content: A rational person proportions belief to evidence, and probability seems to be the tool for doing so, since it measures how strongly evidence supports a hypothesis. Philosophy has nevertheless found the relation between the two harder to state than it appears, because probabilities can be interpreted in several ways and not all of them suit the task. One interpretation treats probability as a frequency, so the probability that a coin lands heads is the proportion of heads in a long series of tosses. This works for repeatable events and fails for the claims we most want to assess, since a hypothesis about the past or about a unique event belongs to no series. A second interpretation treats probability as a degree of belief, which applies to any claim whatever. Its difficulty is the reverse, since degrees of belief vary between people and something must explain why one distribution is more reasonable than another. The standard answer requires only that a person's beliefs be internally coherent, and coherence is a weak constraint that permits confident belief in almost anything provided the rest is arranged to match. Philosophers who find this too permissive add further conditions, and the argument about which conditions are defensible remains the central question in this area.

subject: 중세 유럽의 다리 건설과 통행세
title: Medieval bridges and the crossings they replaced
content: A medieval bridge replaced a ford or a ferry, and the archaeological evidence shows that the crossing usually existed long before the structure. Roads converge on such points across centuries of occupation, and the settlements beside them contain material from periods well before any masonry appears. What a bridge changed was reliability rather than route, since a ford is impassable when the river rises and a ferry stops at night. Building one demanded resources that few local communities held, and the surviving records show religious houses, guilds, and rulers all involved in particular cases. Because maintenance was continuous and expensive, the arrangements for funding it were built into the structure from the start, often as a chapel on the bridge itself where travellers were expected to give. The archaeology of medieval bridges accordingly includes these small buildings as standard features rather than as ornaments. When funding failed, the record shows decay proceeding quickly. Timber decks rotted, piers scoured, and a structure unmaintained for a generation became impassable, after which the traffic returned to the older ford. Historians therefore read the presence of a working medieval bridge as evidence of a functioning institution behind it, and its ruin as evidence that the institution had failed rather than that the route had changed.

subject: 기계의 판단에 대한 책임 귀속
title: Assigning responsibility for machine decisions
content: When a system built from many components produces a harmful decision, our moral vocabulary struggles to locate anyone at fault. The people who assembled it made defensible choices, those who deployed it followed reasonable procedure, and the harm arose from an interaction nobody designed. Moral philosophy calls this a responsibility gap, and the question is whether the gap is real or merely apparent. Those who hold it is apparent argue that responsibility has always been distributed and that we manage such cases elsewhere. A pharmaceutical harm involves researchers, regulators, and prescribers, and we assign duties to each without requiring a single culprit, so nothing new is needed. On this view the difficulty is one of institutional design rather than of moral theory. Those who hold the gap is real point to a further feature. Where a system's behaviour cannot be predicted from its parts even by those who built it, the standard grounds for blame are absent, since nobody could have foreseen what occurred. They conclude that either such systems must not be deployed where the stakes are high, or that we must accept harms for which nobody is answerable. Neither conclusion is comfortable, and the practical response so far has been to demand explainability, which sidesteps the philosophical question rather than answering it.

subject: 정체성 주장과 인정의 정치
title: Identity claims and the demand for recognition
content: Claims made on behalf of a group often ask for recognition rather than for goods, and political philosophy has examined what such a demand amounts to. To be recognized is to have one's standing acknowledged by others, and misrecognition is held to be a genuine harm rather than merely an unpleasant experience, because a person whose identity is systematically disparaged carries that judgment into her own self-understanding. Defenders of this framework argue that redistribution alone cannot address the injury. Giving resources to a group whose way of life is treated as inferior leaves the insult intact, and the resources may even be received as confirmation of dependence. Recognition therefore names something distinct that justice must supply. Critics raise two objections. The first is that recognition claims can freeze identities, since a group must present itself as unified and unchanging to press a claim, and members who depart from that presentation are disciplined by their own side. The second is that recognition can substitute for material change, offering symbolic acknowledgement while the underlying inequality persists. Most contemporary positions accept both objections while denying that they defeat the framework, holding that recognition and redistribution address different wrongs and that a theory of justice needs both.

subject: 고대의 목축과 계절 이동
title: Ancient herding and the seasonal round
content: Herding communities in many ancient regions moved their animals between pastures as the seasons changed, and the archaeological traces of this practice are subtle. Camps occupied for a few weeks leave thin deposits, so the sites are easily missed, and the evidence often comes from animal bones rather than from structures. Teeth record the season of death in their growth increments, and chemical signatures in enamel record the altitude at which an animal fed while the tooth was forming. Those signatures allow a herd's yearly movement to be reconstructed from a handful of jaws. Analysis of ancient sites has shown flocks moving between lowland winter grazing and upland summer pasture across distances of many kilometres, and it has shown the pattern persisting for centuries at some locations. Where the isotopes indicate no movement, the community was keeping animals near its settlement, which implies a different arrangement of labour and land. The relationship between herders and farmers is where this evidence bears most. Ancient sources written from the settled side often describe herders as outsiders, whereas the archaeology shows animals wintering on harvested fields and manuring them, which is an arrangement requiring agreement. Historians therefore treat the seasonal round as evidence of cooperation that the written record obscures.

subject: 공연의 일회성과 기록의 한계
title: Performance and the limits of the record
content: A novel outlives its author because the marks on the page hold everything the work requires, and a symphony survives because notation preserves the relations that constitute it. Performance enjoys no such security, since what a dancer achieves exists only while she achieves it, and the recording that remains stands to the event roughly as a photograph of a meal stands to its taste. This gap reaches well beyond the archive. Because a performance cannot be stored, it cannot readily be bought or accumulated, and therefore it sits awkwardly inside institutions organized around permanent collections. Curators have responded by purchasing instructions rather than events, treating the choreographer's directions as the enduring work and each staging as a single instance. Yet this response imports the very assumption it was meant to avoid, since it relocates the work into a durable text and thereby denies that the passing encounter was the point. Some argue that the loss is itself the meaning, holding that a performance criticizes the market in art precisely by leaving nothing behind. Others reply that this romanticizes neglect and writes off traditions whose practices were never written down. The quarrel matters because it determines which histories can be told, and loss is never neutral in how it falls.

subject: 공예와 예술의 경계는 누가 그었나
title: Who drew the line between craft and art
content: The distinction between art and craft feels natural to modern viewers, and yet it is comparatively recent and its boundary has moved repeatedly. Painters and sculptors in earlier centuries belonged to guilds alongside goldsmiths and joiners, trained through apprenticeship, and were paid by contract for work specified in advance. What separated them from other makers was not yet a difference in kind. The separation was argued for rather than discovered. Writers advancing the claim insisted that certain practices involved invention while others involved only execution, and they supported this by pointing to the learning that painting supposedly required. Their argument served an interest, since a maker recognized as an artist could charge differently, choose subjects, and refuse instruction, and the academies founded to certify that status excluded the trades from which painting had emerged. Anthropologists studying societies without this distinction find makers whose work is judged by criteria that cut across it entirely. A vessel may be valued for the skill of its throwing, for the meaning of its decoration, and for its fitness to a ritual purpose, and no ranking places one of these above the others. What the comparison suggests is that our own boundary records a particular history rather than a feature of making itself.

subject: 민속 음악의 채집과 그 왜곡
title: Collecting folk music and what collection changed
content: Collectors who travelled to record traditional music preserved a great deal that would otherwise have vanished, and their work also altered what they preserved. A song exists in variants, since each singer shapes it and each occasion differs, whereas a recording fixes one performance and a transcription fixes still less. What the archive holds is therefore a moment rather than a tradition. Selection compounded this. Collectors sought what seemed authentic to them, which usually meant old, rural, and untouched by commerce, so singers learned which items to offer and which to withhold. The repertoire that reached the archive was thus co-produced by the collector's expectations and the singer's judgment about them, and songs of recent origin or foreign influence were systematically underrepresented. The archive documents a taste as much as a practice. Later revivals then drew on these collections and treated them as the tradition itself. Performers learned versions that had been recorded once from one singer, and those versions became standard because they were the ones available in print. A tradition that had lived through variation acquired fixed texts, and the fixing came from outside. Cultural historians accordingly read such collections as interventions rather than as records, and they read the revival that followed as a new practice rather than a continuation.

subject: 고대 해안 유적의 패총과 식생활
title: Shell middens and what ancient coasts ate
content: A midden of discarded shells can rise many metres and run for hundreds along an ancient shoreline, and archaeologists therefore treat such deposits as among the most informative sites available. Shell preserves well and it gathers layer upon layer, so each layer holds the debris of a season, and a single section cut through a midden yields a sequence that ordinary settlement soil cannot supply. What these layers record is diet in unusual detail. Species proportions shift as the shoreline changed or as collecting pressure told, and the size of individual shells falls where a bed was harvested too heavily, so overexploitation registers directly. Fish bones, bird bones, and charred plant remains appear in the same deposits, and their whole seasonal round can therefore be reconstructed rather than the marine part alone. Growth lines in these shells even record the season of collection. Because such deposits are alkaline, they preserve bone that acidic soils destroy, and burials placed within them survive where those in nearby ground do not. Archaeologists accordingly find human remains, antler tools, and worked bone concentrated in exactly the places that earlier surveys dismissed as refuse. What was long read as a rubbish heap turns out to be the richest archive an ancient coastal settlement left behind.

subject: 규범적 불일치는 해소 가능한가
title: Whether moral disagreement can be resolved
content: People who share the same facts often reach opposite moral conclusions, and philosophy asks whether such disagreement can in principle be settled. This question matters because our confidence in moral judgment depends partly on the answer, since a dispute that no amount of reasoning could close looks unlike a dispute about how the world is. One position holds that most moral disagreement rests on error about matters that are not moral at all. Parties differ about consequences, about who is affected, or about what a practice actually involves, and clearing those differences would bring their moral judgments together. Evidence for this comes from cases where information changed minds, and the position therefore implies that persistent disagreement marks incomplete inquiry rather than a limit on reason. A rival position holds that some of this disagreement is fundamental. Two people may agree on every fact and still weigh liberty against welfare differently, and no further fact settles that weighing. Its defenders argue that moral judgment involves commitments which reasoning constrains without determining. What both sides accept is that the practical question stands apart. Whether or not agreement is available in principle, people must act together under disagreement, and the arrangements for doing so cannot wait for the philosophical answer.

subject: 관행은 이유가 될 수 있는가
title: Whether custom can be a reason
content: Appealing to how a thing has always been done looks like a bad argument, since the fact that a practice is old says nothing about whether it is good. Philosophy has nevertheless asked whether custom can carry moral weight of its own, and several considerations suggest that dismissing it entirely is too quick. A practice that has persisted often encodes learning that nobody now remembers. Rules about food, about building, and about who may marry whom sometimes solve problems that were never stated, and a reformer who abolishes what she cannot justify may be discarding a solution along with the ignorance. This argument recommends caution rather than deference, since it gives no reason to keep a practice once its function is understood and found wanting. A second consideration is stronger. Where people have arranged their lives around a practice, changing it imposes costs on them that a purely forward-looking assessment misses, and their reliance is a moral fact rather than an obstacle. This gives custom weight without treating age as evidence of merit. Critics reply that reliance arguments protect whoever benefits from the existing arrangement, and that the burden of disruption falls unevenly. The dispute is therefore about which costs count rather than about whether tradition is wise.

subject: 증거가 없을 때의 판단 유보
title: Suspending judgment when evidence is absent
content: Where evidence is insufficient, the obvious response is to suspend judgment, and philosophy has asked whether this is always the rational course. Suspension looks safe because it avoids error, and yet it also forgoes truth, so a person who suspends whenever evidence falls short of certainty will believe almost nothing. The two aims of believing truths and avoiding falsehoods pull apart, and no rule satisfies both. One position holds that the aims should be weighted differently in different situations. A juror ought to suspend where a scientist may conjecture, because the costs of error differ, and rationality is therefore sensitive to what hangs on the belief. Critics object that this makes what is true to believe depend on what is convenient, and that practical stakes should govern action rather than belief. A second position denies that suspension is neutral. Withholding judgment on whether a group is being harmed functions as a verdict in practice, since it licenses continuing as before, so the appearance of caution can disguise a substantive choice. Defenders of suspension reply that this collapses belief into action, and that a person may withhold assent while acting to prevent harm. The disagreement turns on whether belief can be insulated from its consequences.

subject: 사생활은 왜 보호받는가
title: Why privacy deserves protection
content: Privacy is widely valued and yet difficult to justify in a way that covers the cases, since what counts as private varies enormously between societies and within them. A moral account must explain why concealment deserves protection when openness is ordinarily a virtue, and several accounts have been offered. The first appeals to harm. Information can be used against a person, so control over it protects her from discrimination and manipulation. This explains much of what we protect and it leaves a residue, because we object to certain intrusions even when no harm follows and none was intended. A second account appeals to relationships, holding that intimacy consists partly in sharing what is not shared generally, so a world without privacy would have no friendships in the sense we value. A third grounds privacy in autonomy, arguing that a person who is always observed cannot experiment or change, since every trial becomes a matter of record. This account explains why surveillance is objectionable even when benign, and it connects privacy to the conditions for developing a self. Most contemporary positions combine the three, and the practical difficulty is that each supports different limits, so a policy defensible on one ground may be indefensible on another.

subject: 의료 자원 배분의 우선순위
title: Setting priorities in medical care
content: Medical resources are finite, so choices about who receives them are unavoidable, and moral philosophy has examined which principles could justify such choices. Treating everyone equally is impossible where treatment is scarce, and treating nobody is worse, so the question is which differences between patients may legitimately count. The most defended principle maximizes health gained, favouring interventions that produce the most benefit per unit of resource. This is efficient and it disadvantages those whose conditions are expensive to treat, which strikes many as penalizing people for their misfortune. A second principle gives priority to the worst off, which honours a widely shared judgment and can direct resources toward patients who will gain very little from them. Age enters the debate in a way that resists easy resolution. Some argue that a younger patient has had less of a life and therefore a stronger claim, while others hold that this treats older people as having lesser worth. Both sides can point to intuitions that most people share. What emerges is that no single principle survives every case, and the arrangements actually used combine several while remaining vulnerable to the objection that they are unprincipled.

subject: 내부 고발자의 의무와 충성
title: The whistleblower between duty and loyalty
content: A person who reveals wrongdoing inside her own organization acts against expectations of loyalty that she may have taken on willingly, and moral philosophy asks how those expectations weigh against the harm she would expose. Loyalty is a real value rather than a mere convention, since relationships depend on it, and treating it as always overridden misreads what makes betrayal painful. Most accounts hold that loyalty binds within limits. An organization that asks for the hiding of serious harm has stepped outside what any member could have agreed to, so the duty lapses rather than being outweighed. This preserves the value while explaining why disclosure is allowed, and it explains the moral residue that whistleblowers report, since the relationship was real even where it failed them. Conditions are usually attached to this. Internal channels should be tried where they exist, the evidence should be sound, and the disclosure should be matched to the wrong rather than sweeping. Critics observe that these conditions bite hardest where organizations are most closed, since a body capable of serious harm is often capable of silencing complaint from within. That objection is not fully answered, and it suggests that the moral burden we place on individuals reflects a failure of institutional design.

subject: 고대 안데스의 결승 문자
title: Knotted cords of the ancient Andes
content: Ancient Andean administrations kept records on knotted cords rather than on any written surface, and hundreds of these objects survive in dry burials and excavated storehouses. A main cord carries hanging strings, each knotted at positions that correspond to a decimal place, so a quantity is read from the pattern and position of the knots. This much was established early, and it made the cords legible as accounts. What remains contested is whether they carried more. Some cords use knot types, cord colours, and spinning directions in ways that do not fit numerical reading, and researchers have argued that these encode names, places, or categories alongside the quantities. Analysis of large collections has found repeating sequences that behave like labels, which supports the claim without settling it. Excavation context has helped. Cords recovered together with storehouse contents can be matched against what the building held, and where the numbers correspond the reading is confirmed, so the accounting function is secure. For the disputed elements no such check exists, since the ancient communities that read them left no key. Historians therefore treat the cords as a system whose arithmetic we have recovered and whose remaining content may not be recoverable at all.

subject: 아름다움에 대한 판단은 객관적인가
title: Whether judgments of beauty can be correct
content: Saying that a painting is beautiful sounds like reporting a property of the painting, and yet people who look carefully disagree, which is not how disputes about properties usually go. Aesthetics has therefore asked whether such judgments can be correct or mistaken at all, and the answers divide sharply. Subjectivists hold that a judgment of beauty reports the speaker's response, so disagreement is only apparent and nobody is wrong. This fits the variability of taste, and it struggles with how we actually argue, since people offer reasons, revise their views, and treat some judgments as better informed than others. A pure subjectivism cannot explain why we bother. A middle position holds that beauty is a response that qualified observers would converge upon, so the judgment is about the object while remaining tied to how creatures like us perceive. Its difficulty lies in specifying who counts as qualified without appealing to their having the right responses, which threatens circularity. What most accounts now preserve is that aesthetic argument is real argument, and that failing to see something in a work can be a failure rather than a difference.
